lessons.title: The Particle Model and States of Matter

practice_questions.text:
Which one of the following correctly describes the arrangement and movement of particles in a liquid?
A) Regular arrangement, vibrate in fixed positions
B) Irregular arrangement, move randomly at high speed, far apart
C) Irregular arrangement, close together, slide past each other
D) Regular arrangement, far apart, strong attractive forces
practice_questions.marks: C) Irregular arrangement, close together, slide past each other [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: State the name given to the change of state when a substance converts directly from a solid to a gas.
practice_questions.marks: Sublimation [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: Describe how the temperature changes when a pure substance is heated from solid to gas, and explain what happens at the melting point.
practice_questions.marks: Temperature rises as the solid heats up, stays constant (flat section) at the melting point as the solid converts to liquid, then rises again as the liquid heats up [1 mark]; at the melting point, energy supplied is used to break forces between particles rather than raising the kinetic energy of particles, so temperature stays constant [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: Explain the difference between a physical change and a chemical change. Give one example of each.
practice_questions.marks: A physical change does not produce any new substances and is reversible [1 mark]; a chemical change produces one or more new substances with different properties and is usually irreversible [1 mark]; example of physical: melting ice, dissolving salt (accept any valid physical change); example of chemical: burning wood, cooking food, rusting iron [1 mark]

practice_questions.text:
A student heats a sample of an impure solid and measures its temperature over time. She notices that the substance begins to melt at 45°C and finishes melting at 52°C.
A pure sample of the same substance melts at exactly 48°C.
Explain these observations using your knowledge of the particle model.
practice_questions.marks:
A pure substance has particles of one type, all held together by forces of the same strength, so all particles overcome these forces at the same temperature, giving a sharp melting point [1 mark]
Impurities disrupt the regular arrangement of particles in the solid [1 mark]; different impurity particles are held by forces of different strengths [1 mark]; so different particles overcome these forces at different temperatures, giving a range of melting temperatures rather than a single sharp point [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: Explain two limitations of the simple particle model in describing the behaviour of matter.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Two limitations clearly stated with precise explanation of what each prevents the model from explaining; examples given; accurate scientific language throughout.
Secure: Two limitations described with partial explanation; some scientific terminology.
Developing: One clear limitation or two vague ones; limited explanation.
Emerging: Vague statement about the model without specific limitations.

Limitations may include:
(1) The model treats all particles as identical solid spheres of the same size, ignoring that different atoms, molecules and ions have different sizes and masses. This means the model cannot explain why different substances have different properties such as different melting and boiling points.
(2) The model does not represent the forces of attraction between particles. In reality it is these forces (bonds and intermolecular forces) that hold matter together and determine state. The model appears to show particles simply touching or repelling.
(3) In gas diagrams, particles are usually shown much closer together than they actually are — gas particles are typically very much further apart than solid or liquid particles.
[Award up to 3 marks per limitation: 1 for naming it, 2 for explaining what it fails to account for, 3 for linking it to a property the model cannot explain]

before.content_html:
The Development of the Periodic Table

In the nineteenth century, scientists searched for a way to organise the growing number of known elements. Dmitri Mendeleev produced the most successful early arrangement around 1869. He ordered elements by atomic weight but made two crucial decisions that others had not: he left deliberate gaps for elements that had not yet been discovered, and he swapped the order of a few elements so that those with similar chemical properties lined up in the same vertical columns. When subsequently discovered elements — including gallium and germanium — matched the properties he had predicted for the gaps, his table gained wide acceptance. The modern periodic table arranges elements in order of atomic number (proton number) rather than atomic weight, which resolved the few anomalies in Mendeleev’s arrangement.

Key Fact

Elements in the periodic table are arranged in order of atomic number. Elements in the same group (column) have the same number of outer electrons and similar chemical properties. Elements in the same period (row) have the same number of electron shells. Metals are on the left and centre; non-metals are on the right.

Group 1 — The Alkali Metals

The alkali metals (lithium, sodium, potassium, rubidium, caesium and francium) all have one electron in their outer shell. They are soft, low-density metals with relatively low melting points compared to most metals. All react vigorously with water, producing a metal hydroxide solution and hydrogen gas. The general equation for the reaction with water is:

$$\text{metal} + H_2O \rightarrow \text{metal hydroxide} + H_2$$

For example, sodium reacts with water according to:

$$2Na(s) + 2H_2O(l) \rightarrow 2NaOH(aq) + H_2(g)$$

Going down Group 1, reactivity increases. This is because the outer electron is in a shell that is increasingly far from the nucleus, and so is more weakly attracted by the positive nuclear charge. The outer electron is therefore more easily lost. Potassium reacts faster and more vigorously with water than sodium, which in turn reacts faster than lithium. Melting points decrease and densities generally increase going down the group.

Flame tests allow you to identify metal ions by the colour they produce when heated in a Bunsen flame. A clean platinum or nichrome wire loop is dipped into the sample and held in the hottest part of the flame. Group 1 metal flame colours: lithium → crimson, sodium → yellow, potassium → lilac. This is a practical activity group (PAG C4) context — you should be able to describe the method, identify metals from flame colours, and explain why each loop must be cleaned between tests (to avoid contamination from previous samples).

Group 7 — The Halogens

The halogens (fluorine, chlorine, bromine, iodine and astatine) have seven electrons in their outer shell and exist as diatomic molecules (\(F_2\), \(Cl_2\), \(Br_2\), \(I_2\)). They need to gain just one electron to achieve a full outer shell, which makes them very reactive non-metals. At room temperature, chlorine is a pale yellow-green gas, bromine is a red-brown liquid, and iodine is a dark grey solid. Going down Group 7, the boiling point increases as the molecules get larger.

Going down Group 7, reactivity decreases. This is because the outer shell is further from the nucleus in atoms lower in the group, making it harder for the nucleus to attract an extra electron. A more reactive halogen can displace a less reactive halogen from a solution of its salt. For example, chlorine displaces bromine from potassium bromide solution:

$$Cl_2(aq) + 2KBr(aq) \rightarrow 2KCl(aq) + Br_2(aq)$$

If chlorine is added to potassium iodide solution, a brown colour develops as iodine is displaced. If bromine is added to potassium chloride solution, no reaction occurs because bromine is less reactive than chlorine.

Key Fact

Group 1: reactivity increases going down (outer electron lost more easily as it is further from the nucleus). Group 7: reactivity decreases going down (harder to gain an electron as the outer shell is further from the nucleus). These trends are opposite because metals lose electrons while non-metals gain them.

Group 0 — The Noble Gases

The noble gases (helium, neon, argon, krypton, xenon and radon) have completely full outer electron shells. This makes them very stable and extremely unreactive — they do not normally form compounds. They exist as single atoms (monatomic) rather than as molecules. Their boiling points increase going down the group as the atoms get larger and intermolecular forces increase. Noble gases have many practical applications: helium in weather balloons and airships (less dense than air, non-flammable), neon in display lighting (glows a distinctive red-orange), and argon in tungsten filament light bulbs and in welding (inert atmosphere prevents oxidation).

An element’s position in the periodic table lets you predict its reactions. Group number tells you how many outer electrons the atom has, which tells you how it bonds. Period number tells you how many electron shells it has, and going down a group the outer shell moves further from the nucleus. Mendeleev used exactly this logic to predict the properties of undiscovered elements — he predicted the density, melting point and typical compounds of elements such as gallium before they were discovered. The predictions were confirmed when the elements were isolated, which powerfully validated the periodic table as a predictive tool, not just a classification system.

before.content_html:
Pure Substances in Chemistry

In everyday language, “pure” often means natural or uncontaminated. In chemistry, the meaning is much more specific: a pure substance contains only a single element or a single compound, with nothing else mixed in. Pure water contains only \(H_2O\) molecules. Orange juice labelled “pure” in a supermarket is not pure in the chemical sense, because it is a mixture of water, sugars, citric acid and other compounds. This distinction between the everyday and scientific meanings of “pure” is regularly tested.

You can test purity by measuring melting point or boiling point. A pure substance melts and boils at a single sharp temperature. An impure substance (a mixture) melts over a range of temperatures, and its measured melting point will be lower than the expected value for the pure substance. Similarly, mixtures boil over a range of temperatures rather than at a single point.

Key Fact

In chemistry, pure = only one element or one compound. A pure substance has a sharp, fixed melting and boiling point. An impure substance melts and boils over a range of temperatures, and the melting point is depressed below the expected value.

Formulations

Many useful products are formulations — carefully designed mixtures where each component is present in a precise amount. Formulations include alloys (e.g. steel: iron with a small proportion of carbon and sometimes other metals), paints (pigment, binder and solvent in defined ratios), medicines (active ingredient combined with fillers and stabilisers), fuels (blends of hydrocarbons), and foods such as sauces and dressings. Each component contributes specific properties to the final product, and changing the proportions changes the product’s behaviour.

Filtration and Crystallisation (PAG C2)

Filtration separates an insoluble solid from a liquid. The mixture is poured through filter paper in a funnel. The liquid (the filtrate) passes through the tiny pores in the paper, while the insoluble solid (the residue) is trapped. For example, you could separate sand from salt water using filtration — the sand stays on the paper and the salt water collects in the flask below. This is a key technique in practical activity group PAG C2.

Crystallisation separates a dissolved solid (solute) from a solution. Heat the solution gently to evaporate most of the solvent until crystals just begin to form. Remove from heat and allow to cool slowly — as the temperature drops, more solute comes out of solution and grows into larger, purer crystals. Filter the crystals and leave them to dry. Slow cooling produces larger, purer crystals than rapid cooling. This technique is used to produce pure, dry samples of soluble salts such as copper sulfate or potassium nitrate.

Distillation

Simple distillation separates a solvent from a solution when the solvent alone is wanted as the pure product — for example, collecting pure water from salt water. The solution is heated until the solvent evaporates, the vapour passes through a condenser where it is cooled, and it collects as liquid in a separate container. The dissolved solid remains in the flask.

Fractional distillation is used when the mixture contains two or more liquids with different boiling points. The mixture is heated in a flask fitted with a fractionating column. Liquids with lower boiling points vaporise first, rise to the top of the column, and are collected separately. As the temperature is increased, fractions with progressively higher boiling points are collected. A familiar application is the separation of crude oil into useful fractions (petrol, kerosene, diesel, etc.) in a refinery.

Chromatography (PAG C3)

Chromatography separates a mixture of dissolved substances. It works because different substances travel at different speeds through a stationary phase (such as chromatography paper) when carried by a mobile phase (a solvent). In paper chromatography (PAG C3):

  1. Draw a pencil baseline near the bottom of the chromatography paper (pencil is used because ink would dissolve and move up with the solvent).
  2. Place a small spot of the mixture on the baseline.
  3. Place the paper in a beaker of solvent, making sure the baseline is above the solvent level so the spots do not dissolve directly.
  4. Allow the solvent to rise up the paper, carrying the different substances with it.
  5. Mark the solvent front before it evaporates.

Substances that are more attracted to the mobile phase (or less attracted to the stationary phase) travel further up the paper. A pure substance produces a single spot; a mixture produces several spots at different heights. The chromatogram can be used to identify substances by comparing spot positions to those of known reference substances run alongside.

Key Fact

The Rf value identifies a substance and is calculated as:

$$R_f = \frac{\text{distance moved by substance}}{\text{distance moved by solvent front}}$$

Rf values are always between 0 and 1. A pure substance gives a single spot with a characteristic Rf value for a given solvent and stationary phase. A mixture gives multiple spots.

A chromatography experiment produces a spot that travels 4.8 cm from the baseline. The solvent front travels 8.0 cm from the baseline. Calculate the Rf value.

Step 1: Identify the values. Distance moved by substance = 4.8 cm. Distance moved by solvent front = 8.0 cm.

Step 2: Apply the formula. $$R_f = \frac{4.8}{8.0} = 0.60$$

Step 3: Check the answer is between 0 and 1. \(R_f = 0.60\) — this is correct. Note that Rf values have no units. If you obtain a value greater than 1, you have divided the wrong way round.

practice_questions.text:
A student measures the melting point of a sample of aspirin and finds it melts over the range 131–138°C. The expected melting point of pure aspirin is 135°C. What conclusion can be drawn?
A) The sample is pure aspirin
B) The sample is impure and contains at least one other substance
C) The sample is pure but has been stored incorrectly
D) The melting point range proves the substance is not aspirin
practice_questions.marks: B) The sample is impure and contains at least one other substance [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: Name two separation techniques that could be used to obtain pure solid copper sulfate crystals from a solution of copper sulfate in water.
practice_questions.marks: Evaporation/heating to reduce volume, then crystallisation (slow cooling). Both steps required for the mark, or crystallisation alone accepted. [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: Describe how you would use paper chromatography to find out whether a food colouring is a mixture of dyes or a single pure dye.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Describes drawing a pencil baseline, placing a spot of food colouring on the line, placing paper in solvent (below baseline), allowing solvent to rise, then interpreting the result: single spot = pure dye, multiple spots = mixture.
Secure: Covers method and interpretation clearly.
Developing: Describes the method but does not explain how to interpret the results.
Emerging: Vague description of “put it in solvent and see what happens.”

practice_questions.text: Explain why simple distillation is used to obtain pure water from sea water, and why fractional distillation would not be needed for this process.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Sea water is a solution of salts dissolved in water. Simple distillation heats the sea water, the water evaporates and is condensed, leaving the dissolved salts behind. Fractional distillation is not needed because there is only one liquid (water) to separate from a non-volatile dissolved solid; fractional distillation is required when separating two or more liquids with different boiling points.
Secure: Correct explanation of simple distillation with reason why fractional distillation is unnecessary.
Developing: Explains simple distillation correctly but does not address why fractional distillation is unnecessary.
Emerging: States that water evaporates without explaining the technique.

practice_questions.text: In a chromatography experiment, a yellow food dye produces a spot that moves 5.4 cm. The solvent front moves 9.0 cm. A reference sample of tartrazine produces a spot that moves 5.4 cm under identical conditions. Calculate the Rf value of the food dye and state whether the food dye could be tartrazine.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Rf = 5.4 ÷ 9.0 = 0.60 [1]. Units: Rf has no units [1]. Rf of dye matches Rf of tartrazine (0.60) so the dye could be tartrazine [1]. Acknowledges this is not conclusive proof (would need to test in multiple solvents) [1].
Secure: Correct Rf calculated, correctly concluded that the dye could be tartrazine.
Developing: Correct calculation but conclusion not clearly stated.
Emerging: Substitutes values but makes arithmetic or formula error.

practice_questions.text: Paints are described as formulations. Explain what this means, and discuss how knowing that a mixture is a formulation rather than a pure substance affects how it would be tested for purity.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Defines formulation as a mixture with each component in a precise measured amount to give specific properties. Names components of paint (e.g. pigment, binder, solvent). Explains that a formulation is not pure in the chemical sense, so it would melt over a range of temperatures, not at a single sharp point. A pure substance would melt sharply. Discusses that chromatography could separate the dye components of the paint. Evaluates that purity testing applies to individual components, not the formulation as a whole.
Secure: Defines formulation with examples, explains effect on melting point, links to testing method.
Developing: Defines formulation and states melting occurs over a range, but limited evaluation.
Emerging: Describes formulations vaguely without linking to purity testing.

before.content_html:
Why Atoms Form Bonds

Atoms are most stable when their outer electron shell is full. Most atoms do not naturally have a full outer shell, so they bond with other atoms to achieve one. There are three main types of chemical bond: ionic bonding, covalent bonding and metallic bonding. All chemical bonds involve electrostatic forces — the attraction between opposite charges. The type of bond that forms depends on whether the bonding atoms are metals or non-metals.

Ionic Bonding

Ionic bonding occurs between a metal and a non-metal. The metal atom transfers one or more electrons to the non-metal atom. The metal loses electrons and becomes a positively charged ion (cation). The non-metal gains electrons and becomes a negatively charged ion (anion). The oppositely charged ions attract each other strongly — this electrostatic attraction is the ionic bond.

For example, in sodium chloride (NaCl): sodium (electronic configuration 2, 8, 1) loses one electron to become \(\text{Na}^+\) (2, 8). Chlorine (2, 8, 7) gains one electron to become \(\text{Cl}^-\) (2, 8, 8). Both now have full outer shells. In magnesium oxide (MgO): magnesium (2, 8, 2) loses two electrons to become \(\text{Mg}^{2+}\), and oxygen (2, 6) gains two electrons to become \(\text{O}^{2-}\). In an ionic compound, vast numbers of ions pack together in a regular three-dimensional giant ionic lattice, where each ion is surrounded by ions of opposite charge.

Key Fact

In ionic bonding, electrons are transferred from metal to non-metal. The ions formed have opposite charges and attract each other. The compound forms a giant ionic lattice. You can use the charges of the ions to work out the formula — the charges must balance to zero overall.

Covalent Bonding

Covalent bonding occurs between non-metal atoms. Instead of transferring electrons, atoms share one or more pairs of electrons. Each shared pair of electrons forms one covalent bond. By sharing, both atoms achieve full outer shells. A single bond involves one shared pair; a double bond involves two shared pairs (e.g. \(O_2\), \(CO_2\)); a triple bond involves three shared pairs (e.g. \(N_2\)).

Examples: in water (\(H_2O\)), the oxygen atom forms a single covalent bond with each of two hydrogen atoms. In chlorine gas (\(Cl_2\)), two chlorine atoms share one pair of electrons. In carbon dioxide (\(CO_2\)), the carbon forms a double bond with each oxygen atom. Covalent compounds range from small simple molecules (\(H_2O\), \(NH_3\), \(CH_4\)) to huge giant covalent structures such as diamond and graphite.

Dot-and-cross diagrams show the outer-shell electrons of each atom involved in bonding. Use dots (•) for electrons from one atom and crosses (×) for electrons from the other. For ionic bonding: draw the ions in separate sets of square brackets, show each ion’s charge, and show where the transferred electrons now sit. For covalent bonding: overlap the outer shells and show shared pairs in the overlap region. Common examples to practise: \(H_2\), \(Cl_2\), \(HCl\), \(H_2O\), \(NH_3\), \(CO_2\), NaCl, \(MgO\). These diagrams are models — they show electron arrangements but do not show the 3D shape, relative atom sizes, or bond lengths.

A dative covalent bond (also called a coordinate bond) is a special type of covalent bond in which both electrons in the shared pair come from the same atom. This occurs when one atom has a lone pair of electrons it can donate to another. An example is the ammonium ion (\(NH_4^+\)) formed when ammonia (\(NH_3\)) donates a lone pair of electrons to a hydrogen ion (\(H^+\)). The resulting bond is identical to any other covalent bond once formed; the distinction is only in how it was formed. Dative covalent bonds are assessed at Higher Tier only.

Metallic Bonding

In metals, atoms are arranged in a regular lattice structure. The outer-shell electrons leave their parent atoms and become delocalised — they are free to move throughout the whole structure. This creates a lattice of positive metal ions surrounded by a “sea” of delocalised electrons. The strong electrostatic attraction between the positive ions and the negative delocalised electrons holds the metal together. This is metallic bonding.

Key Fact

Metals conduct electricity because the delocalised electrons are free to move and carry charge through the structure. The same delocalised electrons allow metals to conduct heat. Metals are malleable (layers of positive ions can slide without breaking the bond, because the electron sea adjusts).

Predicting Bond Type from the Periodic Table

You can use an element’s position in the periodic table to predict what type of bond it will form. Metals are on the left and tend to lose electrons; non-metals are on the right and tend to gain or share electrons. A metal and a non-metal together → ionic bond. Two or more non-metals → covalent bond. A pure metal or alloy → metallic bond. Group number gives the outer electron count, and period number gives the number of shells — both are important in working out which atoms will bond and in what ratio.

The overall charge in an ionic compound must be zero. Group 1 metals form +1 ions; Group 2 metals form +2 ions. Group 6 non-metals form −2 ions; Group 7 non-metals form −1 ions. To work out the formula: find the lowest number of each ion that makes the charges cancel. For example, calcium (\(Ca^{2+}\)) and chloride (\(Cl^-\)): you need two \(Cl^-\) ions to balance one \(Ca^{2+}\), giving \(CaCl_2\). Aluminium (\(Al^{3+}\)) and oxide (\(O^{2-}\)): need 2 \(Al^{3+}\) and 3 \(O^{2-}\) for a total charge of zero, giving \(Al_2O_3\).

Linking Structure to Properties

The physical properties of a substance — its melting point, electrical conductivity, hardness and solubility — depend on the type of bonding and the structure it forms. This is one of the most important relationships in chemistry: understanding the structure allows you to predict and explain the properties. Exam questions very frequently ask you to explain a property in terms of bonding and structure, so you must be able to link every answer back to the forces involved.

Giant Ionic Lattices

Ionic compounds (such as sodium chloride and magnesium oxide) form giant ionic lattices. They have high melting and boiling points because breaking up the lattice requires a large amount of energy to overcome the many strong electrostatic forces between the ions. They do not conduct electricity when solid because the ions are held in fixed positions in the lattice and cannot move. However, they do conduct electricity when molten or when dissolved in water because the ions become free to move and carry charge. Most ionic compounds are soluble in water because water molecules can surround and separate the individual ions. Ionic compounds tend to be brittle: if a force shifts layers of ions so that like charges line up, repulsion between them causes the crystal to shatter.

Key Fact

Ionic compounds: high melting points (strong electrostatic forces in the lattice), conduct electricity only when molten or dissolved (ions must be free to move), do not conduct as solids (ions fixed in the lattice).

Simple Molecular Substances

Simple molecular substances (such as water, oxygen and carbon dioxide) have strong covalent bonds within each molecule but only weak intermolecular forces between molecules. When a simple molecular substance melts or boils, the intermolecular forces are overcome — not the covalent bonds. This gives simple molecular substances low melting and boiling points. They do not conduct electricity in any state because they have no free electrons or ions to carry charge. Larger molecules have more electrons, creating stronger intermolecular forces and therefore higher boiling points. A very common exam error is writing that the covalent bonds are weak — within the molecule, they are strong; the weak forces are those between molecules.

Giant Covalent Structures

Giant covalent structures contain billions of atoms bonded by strong covalent bonds throughout the whole structure. They have very high melting points because many strong covalent bonds must be broken to separate the atoms. Carbon forms several giant covalent allotropes:

In diamond, each carbon atom forms four covalent bonds arranged in a rigid tetrahedral lattice. This makes diamond extremely hard and gives it a very high melting point. Diamond does not conduct electricity because all four outer electrons of each carbon are used in covalent bonds — none are free to move.

In graphite, each carbon atom bonds to three others in flat hexagonal layers. The fourth electron on each carbon is delocalised within the layer, allowing graphite to conduct electricity. The layers are held together by weak intermolecular forces and can slide over each other, making graphite soft and useful as a lubricant or pencil material.

Graphene is a single layer of graphite — one atom thick. It is exceptionally strong for its mass, flexible, and an excellent conductor of electricity. It is being researched for uses in electronics, composites and membranes. Fullerenes are hollow carbon molecules. The most studied is buckminsterfullerene (\(C_{60}\)), shaped like a football. Fullerenes are being investigated as drug delivery vehicles and in nanotechnology. Their cage-like structure can trap other molecules.

Key Fact

Graphite conducts electricity because it has delocalised electrons within each layer. Diamond does not conduct because all four of each carbon’s outer electrons are used in covalent bonds. Graphene (a single graphite layer) also conducts. Fullerenes (e.g. \(C_{60}\)) are hollow cage-like molecules.

Nanoparticles

Nanoparticles have dimensions in the range of roughly 1 to 100 nanometres (nm) and contain between a few hundred and a few thousand atoms. At this scale, materials often behave very differently from how they behave in bulk form. This is because nanoparticles have a very large surface area to volume ratio compared to bulk materials. A larger surface area means more atoms are exposed at the surface, which can dramatically alter reactivity, optical properties and electrical behaviour.

There are several established uses of nanoparticles. Silver nanoparticles are incorporated into some wound dressings and antibacterial coatings because silver at the nanoscale has greater antibacterial effectiveness than bulk silver. Titanium dioxide nanoparticles are used in some sunscreen formulations because they provide UV protection while remaining transparent to visible light, unlike larger particles which appear white. Nanoparticles of various metals and metal oxides are used as catalysts in industrial processes because their large surface area increases reaction rate.

Because nanoparticles are new materials, our knowledge of their long-term effects on health and the environment is still limited. Their very small size means they can potentially enter cells, tissues and even the bloodstream in ways that larger particles cannot. Some research suggests that certain nanoparticles may cause inflammation or other harmful effects in the body or in ecosystems, but long-term data are still being gathered. This is a genuine scientific uncertainty — it does not mean nanoparticles are definitely harmful, but it does mean decisions about their use must weigh potential benefits (improved performance, new medicines) against possible risks (unknown health or ecological impacts). This type of risk-benefit analysis under uncertainty is an important part of how science informs decision-making about new technologies.

Polymers and Metals

Polymers are very long chain molecules. Strong covalent bonds hold the chain together; weaker intermolecular forces act between the chains. Their properties vary depending on the repeating unit and whether the chains are cross-linked or not. Thermoplastic polymers can be remoulded on heating because the intermolecular forces between chains are overcome. Thermosetting polymers cannot be remoulded because they have extensive cross-links between chains. Metals have high melting points, are malleable and are good conductors of electricity and heat. These properties all arise from the sea of delocalised electrons within the metal lattice. Alloys — mixtures of metals — often have different properties from the pure metals they contain, because the differently-sized atoms disrupt the regular lattice and prevent layers sliding as easily.

practice_questions.text:
Which of the following equations is correctly balanced?
A) Na + Cl2 → NaCl
B) 2Na + Cl2 → 2NaCl
C) Na + 2Cl → NaCl2
D) 2Na + Cl2 → NaCl2
practice_questions.marks: B) 2Na + Cl2 → 2NaCl [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: State what the state symbol (aq) means in a chemical equation.
practice_questions.marks: Dissolved in water / in aqueous solution. [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: When magnesium ribbon burns in air, white magnesium oxide powder is formed. The mass of the product is greater than the mass of the magnesium ribbon used. Describe why the product is heavier and explain how this is consistent with conservation of mass.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Magnesium reacts with oxygen from the air to form magnesium oxide. The oxygen atoms from the air are incorporated into the product, increasing the mass. The total mass of all reactants (magnesium + oxygen) equals the total mass of the product magnesium oxide, consistent with conservation of mass.
Secure: Identifies oxygen from air is added and links to conservation of mass.
Developing: States that oxygen is added but does not explain conservation of mass.
Emerging: States that the product is heavier without explaining why.

practice_questions.text: Explain what is meant by conservation of mass in a chemical reaction, and describe how you could demonstrate it experimentally.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Conservation of mass means the total mass of reactants equals the total mass of products because atoms are rearranged but not created or destroyed. To demonstrate: carry out a reaction in a sealed container (e.g. reacting sodium hydroxide solution with hydrochloric acid in a sealed flask), measure the mass before and after, and show it is the same. The sealed container ensures no gas escapes.
Secure: Defines conservation of mass and describes a suitable method with a sealed container.
Developing: Defines conservation of mass correctly but description of experiment is incomplete.
Emerging: States that mass is conserved but explanation is vague.

lessons.title: Energetics, Reaction Profiles and Bond Energies

before.content_html:
Energy Changes in Reactions

Every chemical reaction involves an energy change. Energy is either transferred to the surroundings or absorbed from them. The key principle is that energy is transferred, never created or destroyed. Two categories describe the direction of this transfer: exothermic and endothermic. Understanding which type a reaction belongs to — and the bond-level explanation for why — is central to chemistry at this level.

Key Fact

Exothermic reactions transfer energy to the surroundings — the temperature of the surroundings increases. Endothermic reactions take in energy from the surroundings — the temperature of the surroundings decreases.

Exothermic reactions include combustion (burning fuels), neutralisation (acid + alkali), and many oxidation reactions. Everyday examples include hand warmers and self-heating cans. Endothermic reactions include thermal decomposition and photosynthesis. Sports cold packs use the endothermic dissolution of ammonium nitrate in water to absorb heat from an injury.

Measuring Energy Changes

You can identify whether a reaction is exothermic or endothermic by measuring the temperature change of the surroundings — usually a solution in a polystyrene cup. If the temperature rises, the reaction is exothermic. If the temperature falls, the reaction is endothermic. A polystyrene cup acts as an insulator to reduce heat loss, giving a more accurate reading. Record the starting temperature, the maximum or minimum temperature reached, and calculate the change.

In everyday life, exothermic reactions are exploited wherever heat is needed without external power: hand warmers contain iron powder that oxidises slowly in air, self-heating food cans use the exothermic reaction between calcium oxide and water, and combustion of fuels in engines releases energy to do useful work. Endothermic reactions are used in sports cold packs and in some industrial processes where absorbing heat from the surroundings is beneficial. Understanding the direction of energy transfer helps engineers design safer, more efficient processes.

In your practical work (PAG C1), you may measure energy changes by mixing solutions in a polystyrene cup and recording the temperature change every 30 seconds. The maximum temperature rise (or fall) gives the energy transferred. Key sources of error include heat loss through the sides of the container and incomplete insulation. Using a lid reduces heat loss further. Always record your starting temperature before mixing and take multiple readings to identify any anomalies.

Reaction Profiles

A reaction profile is a diagram that shows the energy levels of reactants and products as a reaction proceeds. The vertical axis shows energy; the horizontal axis shows the progress of the reaction (the reaction pathway). It does not show time — only relative energy levels.

For an exothermic reaction: the products are at a lower energy level than the reactants. The profile shows the energy rising from reactants to a peak (the activation energy barrier), then falling to a level lower than the start. For an endothermic reaction: the products are at a higher energy level than the reactants. The profile shows the energy rising to a peak then settling above the starting level. In both cases, label four things: reactant energy level, product energy level, the activation energy (reactants to the peak), and the overall energy change (reactants to products).

Key Fact

Activation energy is the minimum energy colliding particles need for a reaction to occur. On a reaction profile it is shown as the height from the reactant energy level to the top of the energy barrier (the peak). A catalyst lowers the activation energy, providing an alternative pathway — shown on the profile as a lower peak, while reactant and product energy levels remain unchanged.

Bond Energy Calculations (Higher Tier)

During a chemical reaction, bonds in the reactants must be broken (this requires energy — endothermic step) and new bonds in the products are formed (this releases energy — exothermic step). The overall energy change depends on the balance between these two processes. Bond energy values are given in kJ/mol and represent the energy to break one mole of a particular bond.

Step 1: Add up the total energy required to break all bonds in the reactants. Step 2: Add up the total energy released when all bonds in the products are formed. Step 3: Calculate the overall energy change:

$$\text{energy change} = \text{energy to break bonds} - \text{energy released making bonds}$$

If the answer is positive, the reaction is endothermic. If negative, the reaction is exothermic. Worked example: for \(H_2 + Cl_2 \rightarrow 2HCl\): breaking bonds = H–H (436 kJ) + Cl–Cl (242 kJ) = 678 kJ. Making bonds = 2 × H–Cl (431 kJ) = 862 kJ. Energy change = 678 − 862 = −184 kJ. Negative, so the reaction is exothermic — more energy is released making bonds than is required to break them.

Key Fact

Breaking bonds requires energy (endothermic). Making bonds releases energy (exothermic). A negative overall energy change means exothermic; a positive value means endothermic.

practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Clear distinction between exothermic (energy transferred to surroundings, temperature rises, products at lower energy than reactants) and endothermic (energy absorbed from surroundings, temperature falls, products at higher energy than reactants). Both profiles correctly described with a peak (activation energy) above the reactant level; activation energy clearly defined as minimum energy needed for reaction. Answer explains that all reactions have an activation energy barrier regardless of whether overall reaction is exo or endothermic.
Secure: Correct definitions and profiles described; activation energy mentioned and placed correctly on profiles; may lack explanation of why the barrier exists.

before.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Exothermic reactions transfer energy to the surroundings (temperature rises); endothermic reactions absorb energy from the surroundings (temperature falls). Examples: combustion is exothermic; thermal decomposition is endothermic.
  • A reaction profile shows reactant and product energy levels, the activation energy (height of the energy barrier from reactants to peak), and the overall energy change. Catalysts lower the activation energy without changing reactant or product energy levels.
  • Higher Tier: energy change = energy to break bonds − energy released making bonds. Breaking bonds is endothermic; making bonds is exothermic. A negative result means exothermic overall.
